title: Simulation
body:
Two different things share this word in the vault, and both are real. Sense 1 is the one
[[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] means; sense 2 is the one [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]] means
when it talks about modelling. They are related only by analogy, so keep them apart.

## Sense 1: one machine imitating another

**Machine $A$ simulates machine $B$ when $A$, given a description of $B$ and an input,
produces whatever $B$ would produce on that input.** This is the workhorse proof technique of
the whole course: to show two models are equally powerful, write a simulator each way.

Every equivalence result in [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] is one of these:

| Simulation | What it proves |
|---|---|
| a [[DFA]] simulating an [[NFA]] by tracking the *set* of reachable states | [[Nondeterminism]] adds no power to a finite automaton |
| a deterministic [[Turing Machine]] searching a nondeterministic one's configuration tree | nondeterminism adds no power to a TM, at exponential time cost |
| a one-tape TM interleaving several tapes on one | multi-tape machines are no stronger |
| the universal machine $U$ running $\langle M, w \rangle$ | programs are data, and it is why [[Undecidability]] is possible |
| gliders in [[Cellular Automata]] wired into logic gates | Life is Turing complete |
| an interpreter running a program written in another language | the everyday version of all of the above |

Three things worth noticing about the technique:

- **Simulation is what "Turing complete" means.** A system is Turing complete exactly when it
  can simulate a Turing machine, and that is how [[Lambda Calculus]], register machines, Rule
  110, and every real programming language get admitted to the same class. It is also the
  evidence behind the Church-Turing thesis.
- **It transfers impossibility, not just possibility.** If $A$ simulates $B$ and something is
  undecidable for $B$, it is undecidable for $A$ too. That is the reduction argument in
  [[Undecidability]] and the reason "does this Life pattern die out" is undecidable.
- **It preserves power and destroys speed.** The NFA and multi-tape simulations cost a
  polynomial slowdown; the nondeterministic one costs exponential. Computability does not
  notice; [[Time Complexity]] notices very much, and the difference is where [[NP-Complete]]
  lives.

A real example rather than a theoretical one: a regex engine simulating an [[NFA]] directly
keeps a *set* of active states and steps them all on each input character, which is the subset
construction done lazily, one character at a time, without ever building the [[DFA]].

## Sense 2: modelling a real system on a computer

Building a program whose behaviour stands in for something you cannot experiment on, because
it is too big, too slow, too expensive, or has not been built yet. The book's chapter is this
sense, and the vault has no other note on it.

- **Discrete-event simulation.** The state changes only at scheduled instants, so keep events
  in a priority queue ordered by time, pop the earliest, advance the clock straight to it, and
  let handling the event schedule more events. Queueing systems (tills, packets, [[Ready Queue]]
  scheduling in [[OPERATING SYSTEMS]]) are the standard target, and the clock jumps rather
  than ticking, which is what makes it cheap.
- **Continuous simulation.** The state follows differential equations, so you step time in
  small increments and integrate numerically. Physics engines, circuits, weather. Belongs with
  [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]].
- **Monte Carlo.** When the system is stochastic, run it many times with [[Random Numbers]]
  drawn from the right distributions and take the statistics of the outcomes. The answer is an
  estimate with an error bar, and the error shrinks like $1/\sqrt{n}$, so ten times the
  accuracy costs a hundred times the runs.

The recurring warning is that a simulation is only ever as good as its model and its random
number source, and both are easy to get subtly wrong. A pseudo-random generator with short
period or bad correlations quietly invalidates a Monte Carlo run without ever looking broken,
which is why [[Random Numbers]] is a chapter of its own.

## Core Facts to Know

- Sense 1: $A$ simulates $B$ if $A$ reproduces $B$'s behaviour from a description of $B$.
- Simulation is how equivalence of computational models is proved, in both directions.
- **Turing complete** = able to simulate a [[Turing Machine]].
- Simulation preserves computability and can destroy efficiency (exponential for
  [[Nondeterminism]]).
- Undecidability transfers along a simulation, which is what reduction exploits.
- Sense 2: discrete-event (event queue, clock jumps), continuous (numerical integration),
  Monte Carlo (repeated random trials).
- Monte Carlo error falls as $1/\sqrt{n}$.
